title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: The fundamental significance of the European events at the start of the nineteenth century lies in the mass movement of European peoples from west to east and then from east to west. The initial impulse for the westward movement came from France. For the French to unite into a military force capable of invading the East, they first needed to combine into a sufficiently large group, renounce their established customs and traditions, and—through the process of war and campaigning—develop a leader who could stand at the head of the coming military movement.

And beginning with the French Revolution, the old, inadequately large group was destroyed along with its old customs and traditions. Step by step, a larger group was formed with new customs and traditions, and a man was produced who would stand at the head of that group and of the coming westward-to-eastward movement.

A man without convictions, without habits, without traditions, without a name, and not even a Frenchman emerges—by what seem the strangest coincidences—from the turmoil of French political parties. Without joining any of them, he is carried forward to a prominent position.

His colleagues' incompetence, his opponents' weakness and insignificance, the brazenness of his lies, and his dazzling, self-confident narrow-mindedness raise him to the head of the army. The brilliant quality of the soldiers in the Italian campaign, his opponents' reluctance to fight, and his own childish boldness and self-assurance win him military glory. Countless so-called coincidences accompany him everywhere. The disfavor into which he falls with the rulers of France works in his favor. His attempts to change his career path fail: he isn't accepted into the Russian army, and his appointment to Turkey comes to nothing.

On his return from Italy he finds the government in Paris dissolving; everyone in it is being inevitably swept aside and destroyed. And by coincidence, an escape from this dangerous position presents itself in the form of a pointless, purposeless expedition to Africa. Again, the same so-called coincidences attend him. The impregnable island of Malta surrenders without a shot; his most reckless orders are crowned with success. The enemy fleet, which later won't let a single boat slip past, now lets an entire army through. In Africa, a series of crimes are committed against the practically defenseless inhabitants. And the men who commit these crimes, especially their leader, convince themselves that this is wonderful, that this is glory, that it resembles Caesar and Alexander the Great, and that it is fine.

This ideal of glory and greatness—which consists not merely in considering nothing you do to be wrong but in taking pride in every crime you commit, attributing to it an incomprehensible supernatural significance—this ideal, destined to guide this man and all who follow him, takes full shape in Africa. Whatever he does succeeds. The plague doesn't touch him. The cruelty of massacring prisoners isn't held against him. His childishly reckless, unprovoked, and ignoble departure from Africa—abandoning his comrades in misfortune—is counted in his favor, and again the enemy fleet twice lets him slip through. When, completely intoxicated by the crimes he has so successfully committed, he arrives in Paris with no plan at all, the dissolution of the Republican government, which could have swept him away a year earlier, has now gone so far that his mere presence there, standing outside any party, can only elevate him.
He had no plan; he was afraid of everything; but the parties seized upon him and demanded his participation.
He alone—with his ideal of glory and greatness forged in Italy and Egypt, his insane self-worship, his boldness in crime and frankness in lying—he alone could justify what had to be done.

He is needed for the role that awaits him, and so—almost against his will, despite his indecision, his lack of a plan, and all his mistakes—he is drawn into a conspiracy to seize power, and the conspiracy succeeds.

He is pushed into a session of the legislature. In a panic, he tries to flee, thinking himself finished. He pretends to faint and says senseless things that should have ruined him. But the once proud and shrewd rulers of France—feeling that their role is played out—are even more confused than he is, and fail to say the words they need to say to maintain their power and destroy him.

Chance—millions of chances—give him power, and all people, as if by common agreement, work to confirm that power. Chance shapes the characters of France's rulers, who submit to him; chance shapes the character of Russia's Paul I, who recognizes his authority; chance produces a plot against him that not only fails to harm him but strengthens his power. Chance throws the Duke of Enghien into his hands and accidentally compels him to kill him, thereby convincing the crowd more effectively than any other means that he has the right to rule, since he possesses the power and the will to use it. Chance arranges it so that though he strains every nerve to prepare an expedition against England—which would certainly have destroyed him—he never carries out that plan, and instead falls upon Mack and the Austrians, who surrender without a battle. Chance and genius give him victory after victory. Everything serves him. He is invincible.

Like probing movements before a battle, the western forces push eastward several times—in 1805, 1806, 1807, and 1809—gathering strength and growing. In 1811, the group of people formed in France fuses into one enormous mass with the peoples of central Europe. As this group grows, the man who stands at its head gains more and more justification for his power. During those ten years of preparation, this man forms connections with all the crowned heads of Europe. The rulers of the world, stripped naked by this man, try to oppose him with the ideals of reason and justice. But these seem weak and ridiculous before his ideal of glory and greatness, which makes no sense yet still exerts its force. In their efforts to show him that his plans are wrong, these rulers eagerly humiliate themselves before him. The King of Prussia sends his wife to seek the great man's mercy; the Emperor of Austria considers it a favor that this man accepts the daughter of the Kaisers into his bed. The Pope, guardian of all that the nations hold sacred, uses religion to promote the great man's power. It is not so much Napoleon who prepares himself for the fulfillment of his role as everyone around him who prepares him for the immense responsibility he is about to bear. There is no act, no crime or petty deception, that he commits which is not immediately reflected in the mouths of those around him as a great deed.

The invasion pushes east and reaches its ultimate goal—Moscow. The city is taken; the Russian army suffers heavier losses than the enemy had suffered in any previous war from Austerlitz to Wagram. But suddenly, instead of those strokes of chance and genius that had accompanied him so consistently through an unbroken series of successes toward his intended goal, an endless series of reverse chances occurs—from the cold he catches at Borodino to the sparks that set Moscow ablaze. And instead of genius, stupidity and cowardice appear, without parallel.
The invaders flee, turn back, flee again, and now all the chances work not for Napoleon but always against him.

A counter-movement then takes place from east to west, remarkably resembling the earlier movement from west to east. There are preliminary drives from east to west—similar to the probing movements of 1805, 1807, and 1809—before the great westward surge. There is the same fusion of smaller groups into an enormous one; the same rallying of the peoples of central Europe to the movement; the same hesitation midway; and the same increasing velocity as the goal is approached.

Paris, the final destination, is reached. Napoleon's government and army are destroyed. Napoleon himself no longer matters; all his actions are clearly pitiful and contemptible. But once again an inexplicable stroke of chance occurs. The allies detest Napoleon, in whom they see the cause of their suffering. Stripped of power and authority, exposed as a schemer and villain, he should have seemed to them what he had seemed ten years before and would seem a year later—an outlaw beyond the law. But by some strange coincidence, no one sees this. His role is not yet over. The man who ten years earlier, and one year later, was considered a brigand beyond the law is sent to an island two days' sail from France, which is given to him as his personal domain, with guards and millions that are paid to him for some unknown reason.
